S3 STORAGE CLASS ADVISOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Is your S3 bucket in the wrong storage class?

Paste GB stored, object count, GB read back and GET requests for each bucket or prefix and get the monthly cost in Standard, Standard-IA, Intelligent-Tiering and Glacier Instant Retrieval — including the 128 KB minimum billable size, the per-GB retrieval fees and the 30/90-day minimum durations that make a "cheaper" class cost more.

Nothing is uploaded and AWS is never contacted. The text box is analysed in this browser and never leaves your device.

Findings

RuleLevelDetail

Prefer a CLI, or want a CI check?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one command — reads a file or stdin:

node cli.mjs analyze rows.csv
cat rows.csv | node cli.mjs analyze - --current standard
node cli.mjs analyze rows.csv --fail-on warn      # exit 1 when a class change would save 20% or more
node cli.mjs analyze rows.csv --json --prices my-prices.json

Get cli.mjs and engine.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install, no network call. More: S3 storage classes compared: Standard vs IA vs Intelligent-Tiering vs Glacier.

What's recognised

InputHandling

Prices are illustrative and dated; edit them with --prices in the CLI. Other regions, volume tiers, free tier, lifecycle transition and PUT charges, Glacier Flexible/Deep Archive and One Zone-IA are not modelled.

Common questions

Does this connect to my AWS account?

No. It reads the rows you paste and never contacts AWS. It cannot see your real invoice, free tier, request mix, lifecycle transition fees or discounts, so every dollar figure is your numbers times list prices you can edit.

Where do I get the numbers?

S3 Storage Lens (or an S3 Inventory rollup in Athena) gives bytes and object count per bucket or prefix. CloudWatch S3 request metrics or Storage Lens activity metrics give GET requests and bytes downloaded. Put one row per bucket or prefix: name, GB stored, objects, GB read back per month, GETs per month.

Why is Standard-IA sometimes more expensive than Standard?

Standard-IA bills every object as at least 128 KB, charges $0.01 per GB retrieved, and bills at least 30 days of storage. Many small objects, data you read often, or objects that live under a month all cost more there than in Standard.

How does it price Intelligent-Tiering?

Data you did not read this month is assumed cold: part in the Infrequent tier and the rest in Archive Instant, the rest at Standard rates, plus the per-object monitoring fee. Objects under 128 KB are never tiered, so they cost the same as Standard. It is a model, not a measurement of your access pattern.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser page analyses the text in your own browser and never sends it anywhere. The CLI reads a local file or stdin and makes no network call.

It prices rows you paste at list prices you can edit; it is not a measurement, not a guarantee of what AWS will charge, and a storage class it favours can cost more under your real access pattern. Test a lifecycle rule on a non-critical prefix first.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get cli.mjs and run it yourself.

Everything runs in your browser. The text you paste is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (analyze_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

S3 Storage Class Advisor · guide

S3 storage classes compared: Standard vs IA vs Intelligent-Tiering vs Glacier

Short answer: the per-GB price is the smallest part of the decision. Object size, how often you read the data and how long objects live decide which class is cheapest, and the rows that look cheapest in the price table are the ones most likely to cost more.

What each class charges (us-east-1 list prices)

  • Standard: $0.023 per GB-month, $0.0004 per 1,000 GETs, no retrieval fee, no minimums.
  • Standard-IA: $0.0125 per GB-month, $0.01 per GB retrieved, $0.001 per 1,000 GETs, billed as at least 128 KB per object and at least 30 days.
  • Intelligent-Tiering: $0.023 / $0.0125 / $0.004 per GB-month for frequent / infrequent / archive-instant data, plus $0.0025 per 1,000 objects monitored. No retrieval fee. Objects under 128 KB are never tiered.
  • Glacier Instant Retrieval: $0.004 per GB-month, $0.03 per GB retrieved, $0.01 per 1,000 GETs, 128 KB and 90 day minimums.

The three traps

  1. Small objects. 100 GB spread over 10 million objects is 10 KB each. IA bills them as 128 KB, so you pay for about 1.2 TB. Moving them is a price increase.
  2. Retrieval. Reading back a quarter of your data every month at $0.01 per GB adds up to more than the storage saving once reads cross roughly a quarter of the stored volume.
  3. Short life. Logs or exports deleted after a week still bill 30 days in IA and 90 in Glacier IR.

Measure your buckets

  1. In S3 Storage Lens (or an S3 Inventory query in Athena) get GB stored and object count per bucket or prefix.
  2. From Storage Lens activity metrics or CloudWatch request metrics get GET requests and GB downloaded per month.
  3. Paste one row per bucket or prefix into the advisor, or run node cli.mjs analyze rows.csv.

Questions

Is Standard-IA always cheaper than Standard?

No. It stores for about 46% less per GB but bills a 128 KB minimum per object, 30 days minimum, and $0.01 per GB retrieved. Small objects, frequently read data and short-lived objects usually cost more there.

When does Intelligent-Tiering win?

When objects are at least 128 KB and you cannot predict which ones go cold. You pay $0.0025 per 1,000 objects per month to monitor, but there are no retrieval fees and cold data drops to cheaper tiers automatically. For 100 million small objects the monitoring fee alone can exceed the saving.

Why not put everything in Glacier Instant Retrieval?

It stores at about $0.004 per GB but charges $0.03 per GB retrieved and $0.01 per 1,000 GETs, with a 90-day minimum and 128 KB minimum object size. It wins for data read once or twice a year and loses badly on anything read regularly.
